questions.question: What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer?
questions.title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
questions.direct_answer: Both are mutable string containers, but StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe) while StringBuilder is not — use StringBuilder unless you need thread safety.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using StringBuffer everywhere out of caution — it's slower and unnecessary in single-threaded code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that StringBuilder was added in Java 5 precisely because StringBuffer was too slow for single-threaded use

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So both StringBuilder and StringBuffer solve the same problem: they let you build and modify strings without creating new objects for every operation, unlike immutable String. Internally, both use a resizable char array.

The difference is thread safety. StringBuffer's methods are synchronized — they use locks so only one thread can call them at a time. This makes it safe to use from multiple threads, but the locking overhead makes it slower in single-threaded code.

StringBuilder (added in Java 5) is the non-synchronized version. It's faster because there's no locking, but it's not thread-safe. In practice, you almost always build strings within a single method on a single thread, so StringBuilder is the right choice.

Both have the same API: append(), insert(), delete(), reverse(), toString(). The common interview pattern is: String for immutable values, StringBuilder for building strings in a loop, StringBuffer only when building strings across multiple threads (which is rare).

questions.question: What are the main StringBuilder methods and how do you use them?
questions.title: StringBuilder API
questions.direct_answer: Key StringBuilder methods: append() adds to end, insert() at position, delete() removes range, replace() replaces range, reverse() flips it, toString() extracts the String.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical StringBuilder usage in coding problems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to call toString() at the end, or trying to use String methods on StringBuilder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show awareness of method chaining (fluent API) — append().append().append()

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So StringBuilder has a small, focused API that you'll use constantly in coding problems:

`append(value)` — adds to the end. Works with any type: strings, ints, chars, booleans. Returns `this` so you can chain: `sb.append("Hello").append(" ").append("World")`.

`insert(int index, value)` — inserts at a specific position.

`delete(int start, int end)` — removes characters from start to end (exclusive).

`deleteCharAt(int index)` — removes a single character.

`replace(int start, int end, String str)` — replaces a range with a new string.

`reverse()` — reverses all characters in place. Very useful for palindrome problems.

`charAt(int index)` and `setCharAt(int index, char c)` — read and modify individual characters.

`length()` — current length.

`toString()` — converts to immutable String. Always call this at the end.

The fluent API style (`sb.append(a).append(b).append(c).toString()`) is clean and common in interview solutions.

sections.title: Key Points
content: append() adds to end, returns this (chainable)
reverse() — great for palindrome problems
delete(start, end) — end is exclusive
setCharAt() — modify individual chars (can't do with String)
Always call toString() to get the final String

questions.question: When should you use String vs StringBuilder?
questions.title: String vs StringBuilder: When to Use
questions.direct_answer: Use String for fixed values and simple operations; use StringBuilder when building strings dynamically in loops or with many concatenations.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using StringBuilder for everything even for simple fixed strings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java's compiler optimizes simple + expressions automatically

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the rule of thumb is: use String by default, switch to StringBuilder when you're building strings dynamically.

String is great for: storing fixed text, passing to methods, returning from methods, using as HashMap keys, simple one-liner concatenations.

Switch to StringBuilder when: you're concatenating in a loop (classic performance case), you're building a string step by step with logic (if/else blocks deciding what to append), you need to modify characters in place with setCharAt, or you're reversing a string.

The Java compiler already optimizes simple `'a' + 'b' + 'c'` into a single StringBuilder call, so you don't need to manually use StringBuilder for one-liner concatenations. But it cannot optimize across loop iterations — that's where you do it yourself.

A common interview pattern: process an array and build a result string → use StringBuilder inside the loop, call toString() outside.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Use String for: fixed values, return types, HashMap keys
Use StringBuilder for: loops, step-by-step building, in-place char modification
Compiler handles simple one-liner +
Compiler cannot optimize across loop iterations
Pattern: StringBuilder in loop, toString() after loop

questions.question: How does StringBuilder manage its internal capacity?
questions.title: StringBuilder Capacity
questions.direct_answer: StringBuilder starts with 16 chars capacity and doubles when full — pre-size with new StringBuilder(estimatedLength) to avoid resizing in performance-critical code.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing StringBuilder can be pre-sized

sections.title: Key Points
content: Default capacity: 16 chars
When full: doubles (new array = capacity*2+2), copies all chars
capacity() = allocated; length() = actual content
Pre-size: new StringBuilder(estimatedFinalLength)
ensureCapacity(min) manually expands if needed

questions.question: How do you convert between String and StringBuilder?
questions.title: String ↔ StringBuilder Conversion
questions.direct_answer: String to StringBuilder: new StringBuilder(str). StringBuilder to String: sb.toString() — both create a new char array copy.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking toString() is free — it allocates a new String each call
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Warn against calling toString() inside a loop — call once after all appends

sections.title: Key Points
content: String → StringBuilder: new StringBuilder(str) or sb.append(str)
StringBuilder → String: sb.toString() — O(n), creates new String object
Don't call toString() inside loops — call once after all building
String.valueOf(sb) also works internally (calls toString)
char[]: sb.toString().toCharArray() = two conversions

followup_questions: Is it expensive to call StringBuilder.toString() multiple times?
